title: A Alibi for the Cipher Again
premise: Juniper Eriksen has spent nine years as a night-shift taxi dispatcher, a man deliberately forgettable since the night his sister's hit-and-run case was closed without an arrest. When a letter arrives confessing to her death—postmarked the day after the driver's funeral—Juniper realizes the confession is genuine, and that the confessor's daughter, a cab driver on his own roster, is being framed for reopening it. Pulling dispatch logs, fares, and the city's quiet habit of looking away, Juniper traces the original cover-up to the police sergeant who closed the case and the garage owner who paid him. At the anniversary dinner, Juniper trades his invisibility for the truth, exposing both men at the cost of the only community that ever tolerated him—and finally claiming his sister's name out loud.
about_author: Jude Halloran is a former emergency dispatcher who spent a decade listening to a city breathe through a headset before turning those voices into fiction. They write mysteries about people the paperwork forgets, and live in a rented room above a laundromat they refuse to name.

chapters.title: The Day After Forever
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Nine years after his sister Mara's hit-and-run was closed unsolved, the driver, Aldous Vey, dies, and a confession letter arrives at Juniper's dispatch booth postmarked the day after the funeral. The letter names no one but describes the crash in impossible detail. Emotional beat: the floor drops out of a carefully invisible life.

chapters.title: Voices on the Wire
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. He cross-checks the letter against his own dispatch logs from that night and finds a fare record someone scrubbed—except one entry survived in a backup tape. His colleague Denny warns him to burn it. Emotional beat: the first vertiginous choice between safety and the sister he's stopped saying aloud.

chapters.title: The Girl Who Drives Graveyard
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. He identifies the confessor's daughter, Noor Vey, now a cab driver on his own roster, who has been asking dispatch odd questions about the old logs herself. They circle each other warily at a diner. Emotional beat: two people raised by silence testing whether the other can be trusted with a truth.

chapters.title: What the Garage Keeps
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Noor reveals her father's final weeks: payments to someone called 'the Sarge,' a repaired fender he couldn't explain, and a locked ledger. She believes someone at Vey's garage is using her father's confession to frame her. Emotional beat: grief curdling into fear as she realizes she inherited a debt she never signed.

chapters.title: Sarge
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Retired Sergeant Callum Brade, now a beloved community liaison, greets Juniper with warm familiarity that reads as threat. Brade mentions Mara's name unprompted—a name Juniper has never given anyone at the department. Emotional beat: the predator showing its teeth behind a civic smile.

chapters.title: Anniversary Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. With the anniversary dinner days away, Juniper reconstructs the night from fare slips, a dead dispatcher's notes, and Noor's ledger, proving Brade closed the case for garage owner Wes Tolliver's money—and that Brade has been feeding Noor's name to Internal Affairs. Emotional beat: the map of the cover-up assembling, along with the terrible clarity of what exposing it will cost.

chapters.title: The Tape They Forgot
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Noor retrieves the backup tape from the impound lot and is followed; Juniper takes the fall for the break-in to buy her time, landing in a holding cell with Brade himself on the other side of the glass. Emotional beat: the invisible man finally visible, and it feels like being hunted.

chapters.title: Confession, Second Draft
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV, intercut with the letter's full text. The letter's final paragraph—omitted from the mailed version—implicates Brade by name, and Juniper realizes the confessor mailed two letters: one to clear his conscience, one as insurance. Emotional beat: grief reframed as inheritance; Mara's death was bought, and the receipt still exists.

chapters.title: A Glass Raised
chapters.summary: Juniper and Noor's alternating POV. At the anniversary dinner, before the toast, Juniper plays the tape and reads the second letter aloud as Brade and Tolliver close in; Denny, choosing at last, broadcasts the audio over the dispatch channel so every cab in the city hears it. Emotional beat: the climax—belonging won not by staying quiet but by speaking, together, into every ear at once.

chapters.title: Mara Eriksen
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Weeks later, the case reopened and arrests made, Juniper stands at the grave and says his sister's full name for the first time in nine years. Noor waits by his cab; the dispatcher's board hums with the night's first calls. Emotional beat: resolution—the price of survival was paid, and what's left is a life no longer hidden.
